Q: Solace Queue With Message Selector Without Consumers but Using Solace Gui A:

As you said in your comment, in solace there are two kind of wildcard you can use in your topic subscription (for a queue).

Example:

One system is publishing articles and orders in the following topics:

  • event/system/v1/articles/[types]/[country]/[id]/prices
  • event/system/v1/articles/[types]/[country]/[id]/stocks
  • event/system/v1/orders/[sources]/[country]/[id]/paid
  • event/system/v1/orders/[sources]/[country]/[id]/validation
  1. The * matches exactly one level
case topic subscription description
a event/system/v1/articles/*/IT/*/* for a queue getting all articles prices and stock of any type in Italy only
b event/system/v1/articles/phone/*/*/prices for a queue getting all articles prices of type "phone" in all countries
c event/system/v1/*/*/*/*/* for a queue getting all kind of event from system
  1. The > matches multiple levels

If we take the above samples:

case topic subscription description
a event/system/v1/articles/*/IT/> for a queue getting all articles prices and stock of any type in Italy only
b event/system/v1/articles/phone/*/*/prices We cannot use the > in the middle, hence the subscription stays the same
c event/system/v1/> for a queue getting all kind of event from system

Here you can find some references to the Solace documentation reagrding topic wildcards:

  • Understanding Topics
  • Wildcard Characters in Topic Subscriptions
  • Solace Message Format Topics

Notes:

  • for MQTT, the topic wildcards are a bit different du to the specific syntax of the topics in MQTT protocol. MQTT uses + for a single level wildcard (equivalent to Solace's *) and # for a multi-level wildcard that matches zero or more levels (whereas Solace's > matches one or more levels).
  • I assume you use the term "Selector" for the queue topic subscription and not directly related to the JMS Selector you can also use (but discouraged) for queue consumption.

Q: Netty HttpClient - response timeout vs. read timeout A:

As suggested in comment from @violeta-georgieva > Netty HttpClient - response timeout vs. read timeout the "responseTimeout" should be used.

Q: illegal sequence 0x82 0x51 for Shift JIS A:

Windows 932

Wikipedia's article for the code page 932 layout is misleading. As per Unicode's mapping from 1998 the sequence 0x82 51 is legal:

#        Column #1 is the cp932 code (in hex)
#        Column #2 is the Unicode (in hex as 0xXXXX)
#        Column #3 is the Unicode name (follows a comment sign, '#')
0x8251  0xFF12  #FULLWIDTH DIGIT TWO

With 0x82 as the first byte of a character the following byte may be

  • from 0x4F to 0x58 or
  • from 0x60 to 0x79 or
  • from 0x81 to 0x9A or
  • from 0x9F to 0xF1 - this last range should be the only valid one as per the layout illustration.

Shift JIS 0208

However, even Unicode's mapping for Shift JIS 0208 sees both bytes as valid:

#        Column #1 is the shift-JIS code (in hex)
#        Column #2 is the JIS X 0208 code (in hex as 0xXXXX)
#        Column #3 is the Unicode (in hex as 0xXXXX)
#        Column #4 the Unicode name (follows a comment sign, '#')
0x8251  0x2332  0xFF12  # FULLWIDTH DIGIT TWO

I should indeed have checked actual documents to see that JIS 0208 supports a lot more byte combinations than the Wikipedia article layout illustration imply.

Conclusion

My validation was plain wrong, as it allowed way too few byte combinations. I cannot verify if the video game image was unmodified as per the 1990's or if its metadata was written with a more recent software, but in the end it doesn't matter anyway, since the combination was even valid back then. I'm pretty sure Sega didn't use Windows on their games, so 932 is not an encoding I have to expect.
